## A short, beginner-friendly AI-and-hardware explainer

IBM groups AI in more than one way. In plain English:

- **Narrow AI** is AI built to do a specific job—such as answering questions or making recommendations—but not to handle every kind of thinking task.
- **General AI (AGI)** is a still-theoretical AI that could learn and apply skills to many new tasks much as a person can.
- **Super AI** is a still-theoretical AI that would surpass human abilities at reasoning, learning, and judgment.
- **Reactive AI** makes decisions only from information available right now, without remembering earlier decisions.
- **Limited-memory AI** uses some past and current information to make better decisions; IBM places tools such as generative AI and virtual assistants in this category.

**Microsoft Copilot**, in one sentence: it is Microsoft’s AI assistant for chatting, creating and editing content, finding information, organizing work, and helping with tasks in apps such as Word, Excel, Outlook, and PowerPoint. I left the Copilot main page open in its own tab.

A useful hardware example comes from Tom’s Hardware’s **“Intel aims at AMD’s Threadripper with its new Granite Rapids-WS CPU”**—also left open as the actual article in a separate tab. Its central claim is that Intel’s rumored/work-in-progress Granite Rapids-WS workstation processor could give Intel its first serious chance in years to approach, or possibly exceed, AMD Threadripper’s core counts in high-end workstations. The benchmark listing cited by the article shows **86 cores, 172 threads, and up to a 4.8 GHz clock**; that is close to AMD’s flagship **Threadripper 9995WX with 96 Zen 5 cores**. The article says Granite Rapids can scale to **128 cores**, while its comparable Xeon 6787P has 86 cores and peaks at **3.8 GHz**; it also reports earlier leak claims of up to **128 PCIe 5.0 lanes** and **eight-channel DDR5** support.

That matters for AI because powerful chips can split demanding work across many processing cores and move data quickly, which helps with tasks such as data preparation, simulations, rendering, and some AI workloads. For the biggest modern AI models, dedicated AI or graphics accelerators and ample memory are often just as important—but high-core-count workstation CPUs remain a key part of a capable system.

Sources read: [IBM’s AI-types overview](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/artificial-intelligence-types), [Microsoft Copilot](https://copilot.microsoft.com/), [Tom’s Hardware article](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/cpus/intel-aims-at-amds-threadripper-with-its-new-granite-rapids-ws-cpu-chip-armed-with-core-count-approaching-the-flagship-amd-threadripper-9995wx-boasts-a-4-8ghz-boost-clock).
